items.title: Congress Just Voted to Redraw Yosemite National Park Boundaries. The Bill Is Heading to Trump’s Desk.
items.summary:
A new law is heading to President Trump’s desk that would shift Yosemite’s boundaries by consolidating land between the National Park Service (NPS) and the National Forest System.

On November 18, Congress passed the Ackerson Meadow Land Interchange Act, a bill co-signed by Democratic U.S. Senator Alex Padilla and Republican U.S. Representative Tom McClintock, both from California.

What Does the Ackerson Meadow Land Interchange Act Do? 
 If the president signs it into law, the Ackerson Meadow Land Interchange Act will transfer 160 acres of Stanislaus National Forest land to the NPS for management as part of Yosemite. Another 170 acres of Yosemite National Park land will be transferred to the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) for management as part of Stanislaus National Forest.

The decision comes after a flurry of debate following announcements for public land swaps and transfers. An August report alleged that the NPS was attempting to execute a land exchange within Yosemite for a private road, which reportedly would have given property within park boundaries to a Nevada-based real estate company. Then, in September, Major League Baseball approached the Trump administration about hosting a game at Grand Teton National Park in northwest Wyoming.

Why Lawmakers Want to Fix Yosemite’s “Checkerboard” Border 
 Lawmakers say the Ackerson Meadow decision will address a problem in federal land management in the Sierra Nevada: the checkerboard of boundary lines. In 2016, the Trust for Public Land bought the 400-acre Ackerson Meadow parcel and gifted it to Yosemite. However, the chunk…
items.t: Congress Just Voted to Redraw Yosemite National Park Boundaries. The Bill Is Heading to Trump’s Desk.

items.title: I Started Surfing at 52 and It Helped Me Survive Cancer
items.summary:
“How soon after surgery can I start surfing again?”

That was the first thing I asked my surgeon upon learning I had aggressive breast cancer that required a double mastectomy.

Fourteen months, three surgeries, and 21 rounds of chemotherapy and immunotherapy infusions later, I have paddled out more than 100 times. I’m convinced that surfing through cancer treatment saved my sanity, and possibly my life.

Surfing made me feel strong and beautiful. So I didn’t want to give that up four years later as I faced down cancer.

I grew up about as far from the ocean as you can get, in the Midwest. I moved to Northern California after college and fell in love with the Pacific Ocean. Every time I went to the beach, I was fixated on watching surfers—but never thought I could join them because I was too scared to try. And once I started a family, that dream moved further out of reach.

Fast-forward to the COVID 2020 pandemic lockdown when the public pool where I swam on a Masters swim team was shut down. I started doing laps in the San Francisco Bay with friends. I’d always been terrified of open water swimming, but after a year of braving the Bay’s chilly, choppy waters every morning, I decided it was time to try surfing. I was already wearing a (three-millimeter triathlon) wetsuit.

The author surfing (Photo: Matthew Berridge) 
 I was 52, the age when menopause , graying hair, and wrinkles can make women feel invisible. My kids had just left home for college. I needed something big to fill that hole in my life. I took a surf lesson, and was hooked immediately. On the drive home from…
items.t: I Started Surfing at 52 and It Helped Me Survive Cancer

items.title: The Tour du Mont Blanc Is Getting New Rules in 2027. Having a Guide Is More Important Than Ever.
items.summary:
The trail ahead of us narrows to a ledge, with rock on our left and a sheer drop on our right, camouflaged by trees. After hearing the now-familiar heavy breaths of runners behind me, I move to the mountainside to let them pass. It’s mid-August, and the Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB), the ultramarathon circling Mont Blanc, is kicking off later this month in Chamonix. We started our own Tour du Mont Blanc in Chamonix, the mountain town known as the birthplace of alpinism, which was buzzing with excitement and packs of runners strapped into hydration packs. Ahead of me, a young man is stopped on the narrow dirt trail, calling out to a friend on the forest slope below. Before I can even turn around, our guide, Jason Day, springs into action, grabs a rope from his pack, and helps pull the hiker, whose pack had tumbled down the slope, back to safety.

Moments like that are becoming more common with more trekkers on the Tour du Mont Blanc (TMB), the 170-kilometer (106-mile) loop around Western Europe’s highest peak through France, Italy, and Switzerland. Roughly 80,000 people hike it each year, and visits are up about 50 percent since 2020. “People can only see the backsides of those in front of them,” Jean-Marc Peillex, mayor of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains, a mountain town at the base of Mont Blanc in France, told Swiss broadcaster SRF. That wasn’t my exact experience for most of the trek, but in a few places, especially near Chamonix, the trail was congested.

items.title: Better for the Sea, Better for You
items.summary:
Canned seafood has long been a staple of the outdoor menu: It’s portable, nutritious, and adds a ton of flavor to simple meals. And it’s not just for hikers and campers. Canned and pouched seafood has been steadily rising in popularity in recent years, thanks in part to its protein, omega-3 fatty acids, and convenience. But while tuna can be a great choice for your health, how do you know if it’s a good choice for the environment?

Thanks to pioneering efforts to establish sustainable fishing practices—and make them transparent for consumers—it’s easier than ever to find options that support our complex marine ecosystems. Here’s why it matters.

What’s Wrong  
 According to the most recent data from the National Seafood Association, canned tuna is the third most popular seafood in the United States. That means a lot of tuna harvested from the world’s oceans, making harmful fishing practices even more harmful due to the enormity of the scale. This puts tuna and other fish populations at risk, and unfortunately, these practices still dominate the industry.

Purse seine fishing, which is responsible for about 66% of global tropical tuna catch, per the International Seafood Sustainability Foundation, can be harmful, especially when used in conjunction with fish aggregating devices (FADs). This method involves using a large wall of netting—up to 6,500 feet long and reaching around 650 feet in depth—to surround an entire school of fish. items.t: Better for the Sea, Better for You

items.title: After a Scathing Report on the Dragon Bravo Fire, the Grand Canyon’s Superintendent Is Retiring
items.summary:
On November 23, Grand Canyon National Park Superintendent Ed Keable announced his plan to retire at the end of 2026, after more than six years overseeing the park.

“As Geoffrey Chaucer wrote, ‘All good things must come to an end.’ So, too, my time at GRCA,” Keable wrote in a November 23 email to park employees obtained by Arizona Public Radio station KNAU . In the email, he confirmed that his last day will be December 31 and that agency leaders are working to identify an acting superintendent to take over on January 1.

Keable’s announcement came just ten days after the Department of the Interior released a damning 65-page investigative report detailing how leadership failures, inadequate preparation, and communication breakdowns contributed to the devastating 2025 Dragon Bravo Fire, which destroyed 114 structures on the park’s North Rim, including the historic Grand Canyon Lodge.

The investigation drew on interviews with more than 70 people and a review of over 18,000 documents, including fire management plans and communication logs.

Keable’s retirement email made no mention of the Dragon Bravo Fire or the Interior Department’s investigative report.

“I have made this decision for very personal reasons,” Keable wrote.

Outside contacted Keable and the National Park Service for comment but did not receive a response as of the publishing of this story.

items.title: The Pizza Oven That Turned My Backyard Into My Favorite Hangout Is on Sale
items.summary:
I wrote about my Gozney Arc XL pizza oven two summers ago , when it became the pie de resistance for using my backyard to get outside more (and for a suspicious number of new friends showing up at my house). More than a year later, I’m happy to report that the novelty hasn’t worn off. If anything, I love it more.

One of my favorite ways to spend a Sunday afternoon, or unwind after a mountain bike ride, is inviting friends over for homemade pizzas. Everyone brings their favorite toppings, we experiment with different combinations, and dinner becomes an activity in itself. It’s dinner and a show, and everyone gets fed. And because we keep ours on a covered porch with adequate ventilation, pizza night doesn’t end when winter arrives. Après-ski pizza parties might actually be my favorite use for it.

The Gozney Arc XL makes it ridiculously easy. It runs on propane (I use the same tank from my grill), reaches temperatures up to 950°F, and can cook a 16-inch pizza in as little as 60 seconds. Its lateral rolling flame distributes heat across the oven, so you don’t have to constantly rotate your pizza. The result is that perfectly blistered, chewy crust I usually associate with my favorite wood-fired pizza joints now in my own backyard.

Gozney makes several ovens , from more portable models to larger, more elaborate setups (many are also on sale right now). The Arc XL hits the sweet spot for me because it’s compact enough for our back patio, still with plenty of room to maneuver a full-size pizza.
